PRESCHOOL · AGE 3 · CLASS 5

Opposites & Comparing

Age 3 YearsClass Preschool 5Subjects Opposites & comparing

Twelve cards in six honest opposite pairs — big and small, tall and short, long and short, full and empty, hot and cold, open and closed. Printable opposite sheets to compare at the table, and a house full of things to compare: this class follows Colors & Color Mixing on the preschool path.

Opposites only work side by side, so show every pair together: the big ball next to the small ball, the open door next to the closed one. Start with the pair your child already feels — full and empty at snack time is a fine one — and let the rest of the set wait its turn.

Start Today’s Class ↓Grown-up nearby, little one on the lap or wandering the room — both work.
TODAY’S CLASS

How today’s class works.

Four little steps, in any order that suits you: a welcome from your teacher, the opposite pairs, solving the opposite sheets together, an off-screen hunt, and a warm goodbye. Stop after any step — that is a complete class, and there is never a score at the end.

  2. 2 Learn the opposite pairs
  3. 3 Solve the sheets
  4. 4 Take it off screen

TEACHER WELCOME

“Hello, my friend — and hello to you, grown-up helper! Today we are playing the opposite game: big and little, full and empty, open and shut. Show each pair side by side, say both words together, and let your child shout the difference. Ready?”

— Your Kiddo School teacher

Begin the class ↓First stop: the opposite pairs.
LEARN THE PAIRS

Six pairs, twelve cards, one glance apart.

Every opposite arrives with its partner: big ball then small ball, tall tree then short tree. Say both words in one breath — “big ball… small ball!” — and let your child point at the difference before you move on. Use the arrows to wander, or simply scroll: all twelve cards are below.

Card 1 of 12
Or simply scroll: all 12 cards are below.

Say the pairs together

  • big ball and small ball, tall tree and short tree, long pencil and short pencil — the measuring words. Hold your arms wide for big, pinch two fingers for small.
  • full glass and empty glass, hot soup and cold ice cream, open door and closed door — the everyday opposites. These three already happen at your house every single day.
SOLVE THE SHEETS — ON PAPER OR ON SCREEN

Solve the opposite sheets together.

The six opposite pairs print two to a page, straight from your browser. Printed, cut and compared, they are the class’s real worksheets — and on screen, every card page can be drawn on directly.

  1. 01

    Print the pairs

    Open the printable cards and print all twelve, two to a page. Cut them out together, saying each word as it is cut.

  2. 02

    Lay the pairs side by side

    Put big next to little, tall next to short. Comparing two real cards is where the word difference actually means something.

  3. 03

    Act the pair out

    Arms wide for big, arms close for small; a tall stretch, a short crouch. Bodies learn opposites fastest.

  4. 04

    Find them at home

    Find one pair in the house — a full cup and an empty cup is the classic. Then draw the pair on the card page with the Write & Color layer.

Open the printable cards ↗Draw on the cards on screen ↗

Every card page has a Write & Color layer: your child can draw right on the card with a finger, a stylus or the mouse, then save the finished work. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

TAKE IT OFF SCREEN

Opposites that live in your house.

Comparing words stick away from the screen, on real things your child can hold, pour, knock and line up. Pick one of these — two minutes is plenty — and follow your child’s lead.

The big-and-small basket

  • Collect two sizes of the same things: a big spoon and a small one, a big book and a small one, a big sock and a little one. Drop them in a basket.
  • Pull them out one at a time and sort into two piles, saying the words each time: “big spoon — small spoon!” Your child does the sorting; you do the announcing.

Fill and pour

  • Sink, bath or a bowl on a towel: fill a cup right to the top and say “full!” Then pour it out slowly — “empty!” — and do the whole story again.
  • Spilling is part of the lesson, so the towel is part of the game. Full and empty are sink words; the cards just introduce them.

Hot and cold kitchen talk

  • Warm toast in one hand, cold yogurt in the other: “warm… cold!” A warm bath and a cool drink work just as well. Your child names the pair; you keep every truly hot thing far away.
  • Say it as a game, not a warning — the word “hot” lands best when it is about comparing soup and ice cream, not about being told off.

Open, shut them

  • Cupboard doors, box lids, books and your own two hands all play this game: shout “open!” and “closed!” together as each one happens.
  • Real front doors stay a grown-up job — slow and supervised. Books and hands can open and shut as fast as your child likes.

Stay close, keep it playful and stop while it is still fun. There is nothing to finish here.

A NOTE FROM THE PRINCIPAL

For the grown-ups.

At three, comparing is body-first: arms stretched wide for big, fingers pinched for small, a whole-body crouch for short. The words settle fastest when they ride on real actions — pouring, measuring, knocking — which is why the games here lead back to your kitchen and bathroom. If your child mixes up tall and long, that is exactly on track: the differences between comparing words take years, and the joy of announcing “bigger!” matters more today than getting every word right. Everything gives calm feedback with no scores, and the match board works with pointing alone.

TIPS FOR PARENTS

How to use this class.

Show every pair side by side and say both words in one breath — “big ball, small ball”. The two words together are what make an opposite stick; a single word on its own is just a name. Let your child do the tapping in the games, even when the answer looks obvious to you — the finger teaches the eye.

Then hand the game over: your child shows two cards and asks YOU which is bigger. Getting one wrong on purpose keeps the game alive for weeks, and being the quiz master is powerful practice for a three-year-old.

Age 3 is a guide, not a deadline. If today’s class was one full cup and one empty one at the sink, today’s class was a success.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · OPPOSITES & COMPARING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Big ball — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson hands your child the grandest word in the whole set — and the secret hiding inside it: big is never big alone. It is only bigger than something, which is why the two ball cards always travel together.

    What is this?

    Big means larger than the thing beside it. It is not a size a ball owns forever: the same ball is big next to a marble and small next to a beach ball. Big is a comparing word — it needs two things, and it names the winner.

    What does it mean?

    A three-year-old meets big with the whole body first and the word second. Arms stretch wide, steps turn giant, voices go enormous — and once the feeling is there, the word attaches to it and stays. The comparison is the meaning; the card simply shows the contest with a clear winner.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs three things: big describes the larger one of a pair, the matching word for the other side is small, and every big thing around the house can be found and named. The bigger the hunt, the better the learning.

    Why this matters

    Comparing by size is the front door to early maths: it is measuring without numbers and ordering without worksheets. A child who can say which ball is bigger is already sorting, ranking and reasoning — the same thinking that later handles more and less, taller and shorter, first and last.

    What it teaches

    Comparison and ordering, size vocabulary, observation (working out what is bigger than what), body awareness through acting sizes out, and the confidence of owning a word that applies to nearly everything in the house.

    Words to learn

    bigsmallbiggersizecomparepair

    Say this to your child

    “"This ball is BIG — fling your arms out wide, THIS wide! Big means it wins the size contest. Now look at its partner card: that one is small. Big and small, big and small — say them together, then tell me which ball you would bounce higher."”

    Step by step

    1. Lay the two ball cards side by side and let the pictures do the first teaching — one ball fills almost all of its card, the other sits tiny beside its big word card.
    2. Say both words in one breath: big ball, small ball. Then flip the order. The rhythm is the lesson — your child should hear the pair before pointing at it.
    3. Act the sizes out: wide arms for big, tucked-in arms for small, switching whenever you call the other word.
    4. Hunt the room together for big things — the sofa, the door, the bed — naming each one big with a big voice.
    5. Hand the cards over and let your child quiz you. Get one wrong on purpose — call the small card big — and enjoy being corrected, because teaching the word back is the strongest proof of learning there is.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: how much of the card does the striped ball fill? Can you see the stripes running across it? Where does the card end and the ball not reach? Which words sit with the ball?

    Ask your child

    "Which ball is bigger — this one or the small one?" "Can you find something in this room bigger than the ball?" "Is the sofa big? Bigger than what?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might throw both arms wide and bellow "BIIIIG ball!", line the two cards up and announce the winner, or start ranking everyone at the table by size — a very correct piece of comparing work.

    Out in the real world

    Big happens everywhere once you name it: big buses gliding past small cars, the big spoon that serves and the small spoons that eat, big shoes and little shoes lined up by the door. Each pair you notice out loud is one more repetition — and repetitions, not lessons, are what make comparing words stick.

    Try it together

    Opposite jumps: when you shout big, your child jumps as wide and tall as a body can go; when you shout small, they curl up into the tiniest ball on the rug. Alternate the calls slowly at first, then faster and faster until the words and the giggles arrive together.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "Show me big with your arms. Show me small. Which ball won the size contest?" Wide arms, a tight curl and the right card pointed at — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Act first, talk second: at this age the body teaches the word. When your child decides every ball is big, skip the correction — set the small card beside it and ask "bigger than which one?" The question does the teaching, and your child gets to be the one who figures it out.

    This lesson pairs with the Big ball flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Opposites & Comparing (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · OPPOSITES & COMPARING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Small ball — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson takes the losing side of the size contest — and makes it the fun one. Small things hide, fit in pockets and roll under sofas, which makes small the comparing word with the best games attached.

    What is this?

    Small means littler than the thing beside it. The small ball is small only because the big ball stands next to it — beside a marble, the very same ball would be the big one. Small is a partner word: the two of them only make sense together.

    What does it mean?

    Small is not a downgrade and not a fixed size — it is one side of a comparison, and which side depends on the company. That swap is a genuinely deep idea for a three-year-old: the same object can change its word when its neighbour changes. Playing with that swap is the whole lesson.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: small names the littler one of a pair, small things can hide where big things cannot, and the opposite word is big. Also, quietly for you: treasures small enough to swallow are a real hazard around babies — the safety note below folds that rule into the game.

    Why this matters

    Spotting small things is observation training. Bugs, buttons, seeds, coins and crumbs all live in the small world, and a child who practises finding them is building the careful looking that later finds letters inside words and details inside pictures.

    What it teaches

    Visual discrimination (finding small things in a busy room), comparison thinking, size words, careful reaching and pinching — genuine fine-motor work — plus the social delight of hiding games with rules.

    Words to learn

    smallbigtinyhidelittlefind

    Say this to your child

    “"This ball is small — tiny enough to disappear inside one fist! Small means littler than the other one. Watch: big ball, small ball. Now bring me something small from this room — something that could vanish in your hand!"”

    Step by step

    1. Set the two ball cards next to each other and ask which one would fit in your hand — then close your fingers around the small one in the air to make the idea physical.
    2. Say the pair in one breath — big ball, small ball — and let your child point to each as you go.
    3. Run the hiding test: the small ball could hide under a cup; could the big one? Mime both and let your child discover why small is the hiding champion.
    4. Send the whole room on a small hunt: find three small things — a spoon, a sock, a bottle cap — and bring each one back to the card.
    5. Swap roles: your child hides a small object in a fist and you guess which hand, then trade turns until the guessing gets too good.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: how tiny is the ball — how much of the card does it take up? What is it sitting beside? Do the words small ball take more room on the card than the ball itself does?

    Ask your child

    "Which ball is smaller?" "Could the big ball hide under this cup — why not?" "What is the smallest thing you can see right now?" "Can something small still be heavy?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might announce "tiny ball, tiny hands!" while holding it in the air, parade small finds through the house, or correct you warmly when you hide the big card under a cup that obviously cannot fit it.

    Out in the real world

    The small world is everywhere: buttons on shirts, blueberries in the bowl, the littlest shoe on the mat. Name small things as you meet them, and let your child be the one who spots the tiniest berry, the smallest leaf, the littlest stone on the walk home.

    Try it together

    Hide-and-seek small: one small object — a ball, a spoon, a toy car — gets hidden in the room while your child covers their eyes. Warm warms and cold cools guide the hunt. Small things hide brilliantly, which is exactly what makes the game work, and finding them is the practice.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "Show me small. Which ball would hide under the cup? Find me something smaller than your hand." The curl of the fingers, the right card and a quick find — that is the word landed.

    Parent tips

    Follow the fascination: most children adore the small world, so let the hunt run longer than the lesson planned. Sit down together for small-object play — a floor seat keeps treasures in hands and out of mouths, and turns the safety rule into part of the game.

    Staying safe

    Things small enough to slip through a toilet-paper tube are choking hazards for babies and young toddlers. Keep the small-hunt treasures away from little siblings, and play small-object games sitting down, where nothing wanders off unwatched.

    This lesson pairs with the Small ball flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Opposites & Comparing (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · OPPOSITES & COMPARING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Tall tree — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson teaches tall the way children actually feel it — by stretching. Tall is upward comparing: the tree reaches past everything around it, and your child will too, on tiptoes, against the wall and back to back with you.

    What is this?

    Tall means stretching upward, higher than the things around it. The tree on the card reaches nearly to the top of its picture, which is exactly what tall things do — they go up past the roofs, the fences and everyone standing next to them.

    What does it mean?

    Tall is a comparing word with a direction: up. Children meet it with their whole body — standing tall, stretching tall, growing up the doorframe. The tree card works because the comparison is visible in one picture: the tree goes up and up and the card has to stretch to hold it.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: tall means going up higher than what is nearby, the opposite word is short, and people, trees, towers and lamps can all be compared by height. Measuring themselves against a wall is the personal version of the lesson.

    Why this matters

    Height comparison is one of the earliest measurements a child cares about — usually because they want to be the tall one. That wanting is fuel: every who-is-taller game quietly builds the ordering and comparing skills that maths will ask for later.

    What it teaches

    Upward spatial language (high, top, up), body awareness and balance on tiptoes, comparison and ordering, self-measurement, and the vocabulary of growing — taller this month than last.

    Words to learn

    tallshorthightopstretchgrow

    Say this to your child

    “"Tall tree! Reach up, up, up — can your fingers touch the sky? Tall means it stretches higher than everything around it. Stand up tall like the tree… now find me something in this room that is tall too!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and trace the tree with your finger, bottom to top: up, up, up — all the way tall.
    2. Stand up together and be the trees: tiptoes, arms up, fingers reaching for the ceiling. Say tall while your whole body says it too.
    3. Stand back to back and hold a hand flat over both heads: who is taller? Then add a teddy to the parade — a proper height line-up needs a short friend.
    4. Measure your child against a wall or doorframe and mark it with a pencil. The mark matters less than the ritual — they will ask to be measured again next week.
    5. Compare the two tree cards and ask which tree the birds would pick for a nest, and why. Answering why is comparing with reasons attached.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: where does the tree start and where does it stop? Does it reach the top of the card or stop short of it? What words sit with the tree? How much of the card does the tree take up?

    Ask your child

    "Who is taller, you or me? Who is taller than both of us?" "What is the tallest thing in our house?" "Can a tree grow taller than it is today?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may go up on the very highest tiptoes and announce "I am tall like the tree!", demand a measuring mark of their own, or line the family up shortest to tallest — correct ordering, done for fun.

    Out in the real world

    Tall shows up all over town: the tall crane above the new building, the tall lamppost, the tall slide at the park, the tall tree you can see from the window. Ask "taller than what?" about each one — every answer is another comparison, done for free.

    Try it together

    Grow like a tree: start curled on the floor as a seed, then sprout slowly — knees, trunk, arms, fingertips — until you are the tallest tree in the room. Add a wind verse where the tall tree sways without falling. The slow growth is the point: tall is a direction, and the body just learned it.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "Show me tall. Show me short. Who is taller, the tree on this card or the tree on that one?" The stretch, the crouch and the taller card — that is the word landed.

    Parent tips

    Revisit the wall mark monthly and make a small ceremony of it: "you grew!" Height is one comparison a child experiences from the inside, and watching it change is deeply motivating. Expect tall and long to swap seats for a while — the line-up games sort them out all by themselves.

    This lesson pairs with the Tall tree flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Opposites & Comparing (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · OPPOSITES & COMPARING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Short tree — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson takes the low half of the tree pair and gives it full respect. Short is not the consolation prize — it is the other winner — and the crouching, curling, ground-level games prove it to every part of the body.

    What is this?

    Short means low, close to the ground — littler in height than the thing beside it. The little tree on the card stands about as high as your child, which makes the comparison instantly fair: neither one is embarrassed, both are just being their own height.

    What does it mean?

    Every comparing word has two winners, and short is the honest name for the lower one. Children usually accept short trees, short pencils and short cups warmly — the word only gets complicated when it lands on people. Keeping it on trees and objects in this lesson keeps the feeling safe and the learning quick.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: short means lower than the thing beside it, the opposite is tall, and the same tree that is short next to a big tree could be the tall one in a garden of saplings. Context switches the word — that is the deep idea, met through play.

    Why this matters

    A child who can say short about a tree without flinching owns the whole pair. The comparing vocabulary they build on objects is the same vocabulary the playground will later use on people — meeting it first on trees, with laughter, keeps it kind.

    What it teaches

    Downward spatial language (low, down, ground), crouching and curling — real gross-motor control — comparison thinking, and the social lesson that size words describe, they do not judge.

    Words to learn

    shorttalllowcrouchgroundlittle

    Say this to your child

    “"This tree is short — it stands low, close to the ground. The other tree stretched up; this one stays down here with us. Can you crouch like a short tree? Down low… hold it… and up! Short is not little-and-lesser — short is just the other direction."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and trace the little tree with your finger, then hold up the tall tree card beside it: which one would a cat jump over?
    2. Be the short tree together: crouch down low, fold up small, balance. Hold it for three seconds — freezing is the funny part.
    3. Put the pair together and say both words in one breath: tall tree, short tree. Then swap the order and let your child lead the saying.
    4. Line the family up by height — plus any willing teddies — and let your child arrange everyone. Being the arranger beats being arranged.
    5. Hunt for short things: a short cup, a short chair, a short candle. Short things are everywhere once the word is awake.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: how high does the little tree stand — does it stay low on the card? How much sky is left above it? What words sit beside the tree? Which card is taller, this one or the tall tree?

    Ask your child

    "Which tree is shorter?" "Can you make yourself as short as the tree?" "What is the shortest thing in our kitchen?" "If this tree stood next to a tiny sapling, which one would be the tall one?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may fold into a crouch and shout "short tree!", delight in being shorter than you, or arrange the teddies by height and appoint the smallest one the short tree — all of it is the comparison, working.

    Out in the real world

    Short lives at child height: the short stool by the sink, the short fence, the short shelf with their own books. Point out that the world keeps a short version of nearly everything for children — steps, sinks, shopping trolleys — and that short has its own whole neighbourhood.

    Try it together

    Tall and short statues: dance while the music plays, then freeze as whichever tree you call — a stretched-up tall statue or a folded-down short one. Switch the calls faster and faster. The switching is the real game: it forces both words to stay awake at the same time.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "Show me short. Show me tall. Which tree is the short one?" The fold, the stretch and the little tree pointed at — that is the word landed.

    Parent tips

    Keep short about trees, pencils, cups and furniture for now — children copy how the family uses size words, and trees never mind. If your child asks whether they are short, answer honestly and warmly: "you are three, and three is exactly the right height for three."

    This lesson pairs with the Short tree flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Opposites & Comparing (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · OPPOSITES & COMPARING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Long pencil — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson stretches a comparing word sideways. Tall goes up, but long lies down and reaches — and the pencil tin on your shelf already holds a whole scale of long, from the brand-new crayon to the beloved stub.

    What is this?

    Long means stretching out from one end to the other — reaching further than the thing beside it. The yellow pencil on the card stretches nearly the whole width of its picture. Long is not about height: a snake stretched on the ground is long, and so is a train, and so is one noodle lying on a plate.

    What does it mean?

    Long and short describe reach, not bigness. A pencil can be long and thin; a hippo is big but not long. Keeping those two ideas separate is genuinely useful for a three-year-old, and the pencil pair does it cleanly: both pencils are the same thickness — what changes is the stretch.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: long means one end to the other end with lots of space between, the opposite is short, and things can be lined up from longest to shortest — which is ordering, the quiet maths inside the game.

    Why this matters

    Ordering by length is early measurement with the numbers left out. A child who lines up crayons from longest to shortest is doing the thinking a ruler does — comparing, ordering, finding the extremes — years before any centimetres arrive.

    What it teaches

    Sideways spatial language (long, end to end), ordering and sequencing, comparison, fine-motor placing as the crayons get lined up just so, and the persistence of a game that can always be re-ordered.

    Words to learn

    longshortlongerendstretchline

    Say this to your child

    “"This pencil stretches all the way across the card — it is looong! Long means one end way over there and the other end way over here. Stretch your arms and show me long… now bring me something in this room that is longer than your foot!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and run your finger from one end of the yellow pencil to the other — long is a journey, so travel it.
    2. Hold the long pencil card beside the short pencil card and say both words in one breath: long pencil, short pencil. Let your child take over the saying.
    3. Play the arms version: hands together in front, then slide them apart — how looong? Long, longer, the longest your arms can reach.
    4. Line up three treasures — a crayon, a wooden spoon and a shoe — from longest to shortest. Shuffling the order again and again is half the fun and all of the maths.
    5. Let your child be the length judge: hold up two things and ask which is longer. Then swap and let them judge you — get one wrong on purpose and enjoy the correction.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: where does the pencil start and where does it end? What color is it? Does it reach across most of the card? What words sit with it?

    Ask your child

    "Which pencil is longer?" "Can you find something longer than your foot?" "Is a snake long or tall?" "Which crayon in the tin is the longest one of all?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might draw a loooong line across paper and narrate it, line up every crayon from longest to shortest without being asked, or slide their arms apart and announce "this looong!" — the word attaching itself to the body, exactly as planned.

    Out in the real world

    Long things hold the world together: the long table, the long scarf, the long road to grandma, the long queue at the shop. Name them as you wait in them — a long queue is a comparing word your child can stand inside.

    Try it together

    Measuring without rulers: how many hands long is the table? Place your child’s hand at one end, yours next to it, and count together — three hands, four hands. Any length becomes countable, and your child has just discovered why people invented measuring in the first place.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "Show me long with your arms. Which pencil is the long one? Line up these two — which is longer?" The stretch, the card and a confident point — that is the word landed.

    Parent tips

    Keep the line-up games short and frequent — ordering is addictive once it starts. And answer the tall-versus-long mix-up with patience: things that lie down are long, things that stand up are tall, and your child will sort them out through the games long before any rule makes sense.

    This lesson pairs with the Long pencil flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Opposites & Comparing (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · OPPOSITES & COMPARING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Short pencil — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson honours the pencil stub every household owns. Short is the comparing word with a past: this pencil was long once, and the two cards side by side tell its whole story without a word of help from you.

    What is this?

    Short means little from one end to the other — not much reach left. The pencil on the card has been sharpened down to a friendly stub: small enough to disappear inside a fist, worn short by all the drawing it has already done.

    What does it mean?

    Short is the partner of long, and the pencil pair shows something rare: a thing that changed. The stub was long once. Sharpening did not make it worse — it made it short, and well-loved. Comparing words describe right now; this pencil just happens to have a then, which makes the pair twice as interesting.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: short means littler in length than the thing beside it, the opposite is long, and short things still work perfectly — the stub draws. Losing length is not losing the job, and that small lesson travels much further than the pencil tin.

    Why this matters

    Ordering from longest to shortest is the game, but the idea underneath is bigger: things change and still belong. A child who defends the little stub at the end of the line-up is practising ordering and kindness at the same table.

    What it teaches

    Length vocabulary, ordering and comparing, fine-motor pencil grip — stub pencils practically force a good one — storytelling (what happened to this pencil?), and the gentle first idea that used does not mean useless.

    Words to learn

    shortlongstublittleendorder

    Say this to your child

    “"This pencil is short — it was long once, and all that drawing sharpened it away! Short means little from end to end. Look: long pencil, short pencil. Now let us line up your crayons — longest first… shortest last. Where does the stub go?"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask the story question first: what do you think happened to this pencil? Let your child guess — then tell them: it was long once, and drawing sharpened it away.
    2. Hold up the long pencil card, then the short one, and say the pair together: long pencil, short pencil. Trace the long stretch of one and the little stub of the other.
    3. Open the crayon or pencil tin and line everything up from longest to shortest, end to end. The stub goes at the finish line — the very shortest, and proud of it.
    4. Test the stub’s job: can the short pencil still make a mark? One proud scribble answers the question every time.
    5. Let your child point at any two pencils and say which is longer, which is shorter — then swap and let them quiz you, mistakes warmly encouraged.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: how much pencil is there — does it stretch across the card or sit small in one corner? Where is its point? What words sit with it? Which card shows more pencil, this one or the long one?

    Ask your child

    "Which pencil is shorter?" "What happened to make this one short?" "Can the short pencil still draw?" "Where does the shortest crayon go in our line-up?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may cradle the stub and narrate its whole life story, place it last in every line-up with ceremony, or hold up a tiny crayon and declare it "still working!" — the comparing and the kindness arriving together.

    Out in the real world

    Short shows up all over the kitchen and the craft box: the short candle, the short piece of chalk, the last little soap. Point out that short things are the veterans — the soap is short because it washed so many hands, the candle short because it lit so many dinners.

    Try it together

    The crayon line-up race: tip the tin out and see how fast your child can order everything from longest to shortest — then mix it up and beat the clock again. Add a referee rule for equal lengths: two the same go side by side as twins, which is real comparing language wearing a game’s clothes.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "Show me short. Which pencil used to be long? Can the short one still draw?" The pinch of the fingers, the story and the proud scribble — that is the word landed.

    Parent tips

    Keep every stub — children defend them, and a tin of mixed lengths is the best ordering toy you own. If a crayon ever snaps and causes grief, this pencil pair is your comfort: it changed, and it still belongs. Tape the two halves side by side as twins.

    This lesson pairs with the Short pencil flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Opposites & Comparing (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · OPPOSITES & COMPARING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Full glass — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson names something your child has watched happen a hundred times: the cup that fills to the top. Full is a capacity word — how much space the drink takes — and the sink is about to become the classroom.

    What is this?

    Full means holding as much as it can — right to the top, no room left. The glass on the card is filled to the brim with juice. Full is not about the glass itself but about how much of it is taken up: the same glass can be full, half-way or empty, and the word changes each time.

    What does it mean?

    Full and empty live on the same glass, one sip apart. That is their magic for a three-year-old: this pair moves. Cups fill at the tap and empty at the table, bathtubs fill and drain, and your child stands at the crossing point announcing each change. The word attaches to a process they can watch and cause.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: full means the top is reached and one more drop spills, the opposite is empty, and pouring is how full turns into empty. Also for you: full glasses are heavy and wobbly — the game below happens at the sink with a towel down, and plastic cups make the best props.

    Why this matters

    Capacity is measurement’s everyday cousin: enough, too much, all gone. A child who watches a glass travel from full to empty is meeting quantity change — the same idea that later becomes subtraction — with hands and eyes already involved.

    What it teaches

    Capacity vocabulary (full, half, empty), cause and effect as pouring changes the level, careful two-handed pouring — genuine fine-motor and self-regulation work — and the pride of announcing the states like a scientist.

    Words to learn

    fullemptypourtopfillbrim

    Say this to your child

    “"This glass is full — right to the very top, one more drop and it spills! Full means the glass is holding all it can. Now watch at the sink: filling, filling, FULL. And when we pour it out… all gone, empty! You just watched the whole opposite pair happen."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and point to the very top of the glass: the juice comes all the way up here — that is full.
    2. Announce the pair at real meals: as you pour, say filling… filling… full! Then drink down together, narrating sipping… sipping… empty!
    3. Take the game to the sink with a towel down and two plastic cups: fill one right to the brim and say full — one more drop and it spills.
    4. Pour slowly from the full cup into the empty one and let your child call the changes: going down… going up… swapped!
    5. Hand over the jug and let your child do the filling, stopping at full without spilling. Missing the top by a little is fine — the target is the word, not the watermark.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: how high does the juice come — does it reach the top of the glass? What is the drink? What words sit beside the glass? Is there any room left for more?

    Ask your child

    "Is the glass full or empty?" "What happens if we pour one more drop into a full glass?" "How does a glass get empty?" "What other things can be full — a bath? a box? your tummy?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may announce "full!" at the water tap with enormous pride, narrate an entire cup from filling to empty at dinner, or hold up a finished cup at breakfast and report "all gone — it is empty!" — the vocabulary running on its own schedule now.

    Out in the real world

    Full and empty mark the day: the full kettle, the empty lunchbox after school, the full fuel gauge, the empty shopping bag that has just been unpacked. Name the states as you pass them — a full washing basket and an empty one are the same word pair, living in the hallway.

    Try it together

    The fill-and-pour station: a sink or a basin, a towel, a jug and several plastic cups of different sizes. Your child fills each to full, pours them into each other, and calls out full, half, empty as the levels move. It is water play with a dictionary hidden inside — and the towel keeps the whole thing cheerful.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "Show me full with the cup. Show me empty. What happens with one more drop?" The brim, the cup held upside down and the spill warning — that is the word landed.

    Parent tips

    Put a towel down before the game starts and treat spills as part of the science — a scolding about water on the floor ends the vocabulary practice instantly. Plastic cups for the game, glass for the picture: the card can be fragile so the hands do not have to be.

    Staying safe

    Water on the floor is slippery the moment it lands — the towel goes down first and any spill gets wiped at once, before the next dash across the kitchen. Use plastic cups for the pouring game, and keep the real glass full for looking at, not carrying.

    This lesson pairs with the Full glass flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Opposites & Comparing (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · OPPOSITES & COMPARING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Empty glass — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson takes your child’s oldest announcement — all gone! — and gives it its grown-up name. Empty is the bottom of the glass and the end of the story, and filling it again is the part children love most.

    What is this?

    Empty means nothing left inside — every drop gone. The glass on the card has given everything away. Empty is not sad and not broken: it is a state, the same glass at the end of its drink, ready to be filled again.

    What does it mean?

    Empty is the finishing line of every drink, and your child has been announcing it forever — as all done, as all gone, as a tipped-up cup held to your face. This lesson gives the old discovery its proper name, then shows the best part: empty is not the end, it is the turn. Fill it again, and the pair starts over.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: empty means nothing is left, the opposite is full, and empty things are ready to be filled — cups, boxes, drawers, the bath. The refill is the payoff: your child announces empty, then causes the full.

    Why this matters

    Empty is one of the first quantity words a child truly owns because they have felt it — the finished cup, the box with nothing inside. Naming what they already know builds the habit of noticing quantities everywhere, which is number sense in its work clothes.

    What it teaches

    Quantity vocabulary (empty, all gone, nothing left), cause and effect as refilling reverses the state, memory and prediction — will it be empty if I drink it all? — plus the language pride of owning a grown-up word for an old discovery.

    Words to learn

    emptyfullgonerefilldropagain

    Say this to your child

    “"This glass is empty — every last drop gone, nothing left at all! Empty means nothing is inside anymore. You already knew this word: it is all gone, with its grown-up name. Now — shall we fill it again? Filling, filling… FULL! Empty always gets another turn."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and mime tipping it gently: nothing falls out — it is empty, all gone.
    2. Read the story backwards from breakfast: the juice started full, and sip by sip it arrived here. Empty is where drinks end up.
    3. Play the announcement game at the next meal: your child calls empty! the moment the cup is finished, and you fill it again with ceremony.
    4. Hunt the house for empty things: an empty box, an empty laundry basket, your own empty hands held up palms-out.
    5. Let your child do the refilling at the tap and announce the return trip — filling, filling, full! The loop, run twice, is the lesson learned.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: is there any juice left in the glass? How can you tell it is empty — what would a full glass show instead? What words sit with the glass? If we tipped it, would anything pour out?

    Ask your child

    "Is the glass full or empty?" "How did the juice get finished?" "What can we do to make it full again?" "What else in this house is empty right now?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may hold up the finished cup and announce "empty!" before you can ask, hunt for empty boxes on demand, or report at the bath "the water is going down — getting emptier!" — the word reaching for new situations all by itself.

    Out in the real world

    Empty is a household weather report: the empty biscuit tin (a small tragedy), the empty parking space (a small triumph), the empty phone battery. Say the word as you meet it — empty is one of the rare comparing words the whole adult world uses hourly.

    Try it together

    Fill-it-again: give your child an empty cup, an empty jug and a jug of water at the sink. Their job: make the empty cup full, then empty it back, then narrate both trips. Repeat with an empty bowl, an empty box, an empty bucket — the word doing repetitions across different containers.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "Show me empty. What does empty mean? How do we make it full again?" The upside-down cup, the definition and the march to the tap — that is the word landed.

    Parent tips

    Accept every version of the word — all done, all gone, finished — then offer the upgrade gently: "yes, it is empty!" The old words are the bridge, not the enemy. Keep the refill within your child’s reach; the announcement matters more when they can also cause the answer.

    This lesson pairs with the Empty glass flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Opposites & Comparing (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · OPPOSITES & COMPARING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Hot soup — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson teaches hot carefully, the way children actually meet it: in a serious grown-up voice. Hot is a comparing word with a warning attached — and this card lets your child own the word from a completely safe distance.

    What is this?

    Hot means much warmer than your body — so warm it could hurt to touch. The soup on the card is steaming: the curls above the bowl are the heat escaping, showing itself. Hot is a feeling your skin knows first and your vocabulary learns second.

    What does it mean?

    Steam is the picture’s biggest gift: it is visible heat. Children cannot see warmth, but they can see steam rising from soup, from a kettle, from a bath — which makes hot one of the few safety words with a built-in signal. Learn to read the steam, and the word starts protecting its owner.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: hot means do-not-touch until a grown-up says otherwise, steam means the hot is escaping and the thing is still hot, real hot things — soup, tea, kettles, stoves — are grown-up jobs, and the opposite word is cold. The blowing game below practises the cooling ritual safely.

    Why this matters

    Hot is one of the words parents say in a different voice, and children notice. Owning the word — saying it themselves, spotting the steam, announcing it — turns a vague grown-up alarm into a rule they can read for themselves. That is real safety power for a three-year-old.

    What it teaches

    Temperature vocabulary (hot, warm, cold), reading signals (steam as visible heat), self-protective caution paired with confidence, oral-motor practice in the gentle blowing, and the discipline of a pretend game that stays pretend.

    Words to learn

    hotsteamwarmcoolblowcareful

    Say this to your child

    “"Hot soup — careful, hot! See the steam? That is the heat escaping, telling us to wait. We send soft little breezes at it — whoosh, whoosh — until a grown-up says it is ready. Hot things are grown-up jobs to touch, but you are the boss of the blowing. And the opposite of hot? Cold ice cream — brrr!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and point to the curls above the bowl: that is steam — the heat sneaking out. Steam means the soup is hot.
    2. Say the pair with your voice: hot soup in a serious voice, cold ice cream in a shivery one. The voice is part of the vocabulary.
    3. Play the blowing round over make-believe soup: hands cupped around nothing, gentle whoosh-whoosh blows, then a pretend taste — perfect temperature, delicious.
    4. Teach the ritual: real hot food gets blown, then a tiny test taste by a grown-up, then it is ready. Your child gets to do the blowing every single time.
    5. Walk the kitchen and name the hot things from a safe distance: the kettle, the oven, the pot on the stove. Hot is a kitchen map as well as a word.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: what is rising above the bowl? Where does the steam go — does it fade as it climbs? What words sit with the soup? Does the bowl look full?

    Ask your child

    "What does the steam tell us?" "What do we do before tasting hot soup?" "Who touches the hot things in our kitchen?" "What is the opposite of hot?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may blow fiercely on make-believe soup at every meal and wait, proudly, for the verdict, spot steam rising from the bath and announce "hot! wait!", or shiver dramatically on cue: "cold ice cream — brrr!"

    Out in the real world

    Steam is everywhere once you read it: the kettle, the shower, the pot of pasta, a warm loaf of bread. Each sighting is a repetition of the safety rule — steam means hot, and hot means wait for a grown-up.

    Try it together

    Pretend restaurant: a bowl, a spoon and a lot of imagination. The waiter brings "soup" — your child blows it cool, tastes, announces hot! or just right! — then serves you. Swap seats so they are the customer too; the ritual is what gets practised, safely, at both chairs.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What does steam mean? What do we do before tasting hot soup? Who touches the hot things?" The answer "wait and blow", the ritual and the grown-up rule — that is the word landed.

    Parent tips

    Keep your serious voice for real hot moments only — if everything is hot, nothing is. The card, the pretend soup and the blowing game let the word be playful while the rule stays firm. Give your child the blowing job at every real meal: a ritual they own is a ritual they keep.

    Staying safe

    Real soup, tea, kettles, pots and the stove are grown-up territory — pot handles turned inward, hot drinks out of reach, and your child’s chair well back while anything hot pours or steams. The blowing is theirs; the touching and the pouring are yours.

    This lesson pairs with the Hot soup flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Opposites & Comparing (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · OPPOSITES & COMPARING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Cold ice cream — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson takes the coldest picture in the set and pairs it with the warmest word. Cold is a whole-body feeling — children shiver it, say it and eat it — and the freezer holds the prop that makes the word land in ten seconds flat.

    What is this?

    Cold means much cooler than your body — the kind of temperature that makes you shiver and hurry. The ice cream on the card has three frosty scoops. Cold is a feeling your skin reports instantly: the cold spoon, the cold milk, the cold hands after a snowball.

    What does it mean?

    Cold and hot are a contest, and room temperature usually wins: ice cream melts because the air around it is warmer than the freezer was. That small piece of science — cold loses to warm over time — is visible on a plate in ten minutes, and a three-year-old can watch the whole argument happen.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: cold means the shivery temperature, the opposite is hot, and cold things warm up once they leave the cold place — which is why ice cream must be eaten quickly. The spoon game below gives the feeling a safe, ten-second home.

    Why this matters

    Temperature words are feeling words, and feelings teach fast. A child who can name cold, warm and hot is not just comparing — they are building the vocabulary of their own sensations, which later turns into dressing sensibly, testing a bath with a toe and understanding the kitchen rules.

    What it teaches

    Temperature vocabulary, body awareness (where do I feel cold?), observation of change as ice melts, self-regulation in the shiver-and-freeze game, and the honest first physics of warmth winning over time.

    Words to learn

    coldicemeltshiverfreezewarm

    Say this to your child

    “"Cold ice cream — brrr! Let me see your shivery wiggle! Cold means icy, straight from the freezer. And here is the secret: cold things melt when it is warm — that is why we eat ice cream quickly! Hot soup steams on one card, cold ice cream shivers on the other. Hot and cold, the two ends of everything."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and shiver on cue: brrr! Three scoops, straight from the coldest place in the house.
    2. Say the pair with your bodies: arms wrapped tight for cold, fanning yourselves for hot. The shiver and the fan are the two halves of the word pair.
    3. Run the ten-second feeling game: a cold spoon straight from the freezer in one hand — cold! — then both hands wrapped around a warm mug — warm! Your child just met the whole scale in half a minute.
    4. Set an ice cube on a plate and visit it together every few minutes: smaller… puddle… gone. Cold things melt when they leave the cold place.
    5. Read the pair across both cards: steaming soup on one, frosty scoops on the other. Ask which one your child would eat in summer, and which in winter.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: how many scoops are in the bowl? Do they look frosty or melting? What words sit with the ice cream? Which card is warmer, this one or the hot soup?

    Ask your child

    "What does cold feel like — where do you feel it first?" "Why do we eat ice cream quickly?" "What happens to an ice cube in a warm room?" "What is the opposite of cold?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may deliver an award-winning shiver on the word cold, press a cold spoon to their cheek and report the temperature with scientific gravity, or narrate a melting cube: "it is getting smaller… now it is water!"

    Out in the real world

    Cold is a daily weather report: cold milk from the fridge, the cold tap and the warm one, cold hands in winter, the freezer with its icy breath. Name the temperatures as you move through them — the fridge and the freezer are a two-step field trip.

    Try it together

    The shiver game: dance warm and wiggly until you call cold! — then everyone freezes into a tight shivery ball with their best brrr face. Call hot! and it is loose wiggles again. The switching keeps both temperature words awake, and the freeze is the part they will beg to repeat.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "Show me cold. Show me hot. What happens to ice cream in a warm room?" The shiver, the fan and the melting answer — that is the word landed.

    Parent tips

    The freezer spoon is the whole lesson compressed into ten seconds — keep it as a regular mini-game, not a one-off. And let the melting cube run its full course at least once: watching cold lose to warm, unaided, is your child’s first self-narrated experiment.

    Staying safe

    Ice and frozen spoons are ten-second visitors — holding something frozen for a long time makes little fingers ache, and the ache arrives after the fun has already peaked. Keep the feeling games short, and keep real ice cream for eating, not for holding.

    This lesson pairs with the Cold ice cream flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Opposites & Comparing (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · OPPOSITES & COMPARING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Open door — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson takes the welcoming half of the door pair — the door standing wide — and teaches open as both a comparing word and a doing word. Your child’s hands have been opening things all day; now the word arrives to meet them.

    What is this?

    Open means wide apart, with the way in showing. The door on the card stands wide open — you could walk straight through it. Open is a position word for doors and windows, and a doing word for everything else: books open, boxes open, eyes open, mouths open at every meal.

    What does it mean?

    Open is the word for the moment something becomes passable — the door lets people through, the book lets the story start, the box lets the present out. Children meet open dozens of times a day and love the moment; the card simply names it. Its partner, closed, is the same door at rest.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: open means the way in is showing, the opposite is closed, and doors open with pushes or pulls — some so heavy that grown-ups do the opening. The finger rule below is the serious part of this lesson: doors are strong and little fingers go where doors close.

    Why this matters

    Open and closed describe the state of half the household world — taps, curtains, cupboards, shops. A child who can name and manage openings gains real independence: opening their own lunchbox, their own book, their own coat buttons. The door is just the loudest example.

    What it teaches

    Position vocabulary (open, shut, wide), cause and effect as pushes and pulls move doors, turn-taking in the open-and-shut games, and careful hands — the finger-awareness that real doors quietly demand.

    Words to learn

    openshutwidedoorpushpull

    Say this to your child

    “"This door is open — standing wide, ready for visitors! Open means the way in is showing. Open your hands wide like a door… now shut them! Books open, boxes open, doors open — and what closes them again? Closed! The same door, resting."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card: the door is standing wide — what can come through it? Ask what would happen if it were shut instead.
    2. Say the pair with your hands: fingers spread wide for open, pressed together for shut. Open… shut… open… shut — the hands learn it first.
    3. Try the fastest door in the house: a book. Fling it wide — open! Fold it shut — closed! Then a box lid, then a cupboard.
    4. Visit the real door together — and let the grown-up work it. Push it wide: open! Swing it slow: shut! Your child calls the states; you move the wood.
    5. Walk the house and count the open things you find — the open curtains, the open window — naming each one as you go.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: is the door wide or only partly open? Which way does it swing — can you tell? What words sit with the door? Could somebody walk through it right now?

    Ask your child

    "Is the door open or closed?" "What kinds of things open besides doors?" "How do we open a heavy door safely?" "What is the opposite of open?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may spread both arms wide and announce "open door!", run the open-shut hands game unprompted, or report the household door states like a little guard: "front door closed, cupboard open!"

    Out in the real world

    Open is a town-wide word: the open shop, the open gate, the open window on the bus. Point out which doors you may walk through and which stay closed to visitors — the word quietly teaches public rules as well as positions.

    Try it together

    Open-and-shut everything: ten minutes of deliberately opening and closing whatever is safe — books, boxes, tins with lids, your hands, an umbrella. Narrate each state in one breath — open… shut — and finish with the hand-door game: fingers wide, fingers pressed, faster and faster.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "Show me open with your hands. Show me shut. Is this door open or closed?" The spread, the press and the right answer — that is the word landed.

    Parent tips

    The real door stays a grown-up job: heavy doors swing with more force than small arms expect, and the flashcard can do the dramatic slamming in imagination instead. Let your child call the states while you do the moving — the vocabulary is theirs to own even while the hinge is yours to manage.

    Staying safe

    Doors and little fingers need respect: keep fingers away from the edge and the hinge side where doors close, move doors slowly, and let a grown-up handle the heavy ones. If a baby sibling is crawling nearby, the door game happens in another room.

    This lesson pairs with the Open door flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Opposites & Comparing (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · OPPOSITES & COMPARING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Closed door — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson closes the door pair properly. Closed is the door at rest — shut tight, keeping warmth or quiet or privacy inside — and it comes with the politest rule in the set: when a door is closed, we knock and wait.

    What is this?

    Closed means shut all the way, with no gap showing. The door on the card is closed tight: nobody is walking through it right now. Closed is the resting position of doors, cupboards, boxes and books — the way things are when they are not open.

    What does it mean?

    Doors close for reasons, and each reason is a small life lesson: to keep warmth in, to keep noise out, to give someone privacy, to keep a pet in one room. A closed door is not an ending — it is the door doing a job. And it always answers to a knock and a handle.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: closed means shut all the way, the opposite is open, a closed door gets a knock first, and doors close with slow hands — never a slam. The knock-and-wait habit starts here, at three, and lasts a lifetime.

    Why this matters

    Knocking before entering is one of the earliest real courtesies a child can offer. It teaches waiting, respect for other people’s space and the impulse control of a paused hand — and the closed door gives the habit a clear, visible cue to attach to.

    What it teaches

    Position vocabulary, politeness rituals (knock, wait, listen), slow-and-gentle motor control — the anti-slam training — plus the social idea that some spaces belong to someone even when nobody is inside them.

    Words to learn

    closedopenknockwaitslowshut

    Say this to your child

    “"This door is closed — shut all the way, resting. When a door is closed, we knock: knock knock — may I come in? And we wait for the answer. Doors close slowly, with gentle hands, never with a bang. Open and closed, the same door, doing different jobs."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card: the door is shut tight. Ask what might be happening behind a closed door — quiet, privacy, a nap, a secret.
    2. Say the pair: open door, closed door — arms wide, then palms pressed. Let your child lead the switching.
    3. Practise the knock: knuckle gently on the table, the floor, a book cover — knock knock, may I come in? The rhythm makes it a game; the words make it a courtesy.
    4. Walk the house and find the closed things: the closed cupboard, the closed curtains, the closed washing machine. Each one is shut for a reason — guess the reason together.
    5. Play the slow-hands rule on a real door you choose together: open it slowly, close it slowly, no bang. Slow hands get the job every time.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: is there any gap under or around the door? Could anyone walk through it right now? What words sit with the door? How is this card different from the open door card?

    Ask your child

    "Is the door open or closed?" "What do we do before opening a closed door?" "Why do we close doors slowly?" "What is the opposite of closed?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may knock on every closed door in the house and wait theatrically for permission, close cupboard doors with exaggerated slow-motion hands, or answer your table-knock with a solemn "come in!" — the ritual running on its own now.

    Out in the real world

    Closed doors manage the whole day: the bathroom door closed for privacy, the bedroom door closed for a sleeping baby, the shop door closed on Mondays. Say why each one is shut — closed is a word that comes with a story attached.

    Try it together

    Knock-knock theatre: you sit behind a chair as the closed door, your child knocks — "knock knock, may I come in?" — and you answer in silly voices: "come in, we are having a tea party!" Swap seats so your child is the door too. The knocking, the asking and the waiting all get rehearsed, and the giggles are free.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "Show me closed. What do we do before opening a closed door? Fast hands or slow hands on doors?" The pressed palms, the knock and the word slow — that is the word landed.

    Parent tips

    Honour your child’s own closed doors — a blanket over a table is a house with a door, and knocking on it respects the same rule you are teaching. Children protect rules they see the grown-ups follow, so knock on theirs first.

    Staying safe

    Doors close with force: fingers stay far from the edges and hinges, doors move with slow hands, and slamming is a no for the door and the fingers both. A closed door might have someone behind it — knocking first is the polite rule and the safe one.

    This lesson pairs with the Closed door flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Opposites & Comparing (Preschool).
